extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travel literature / travelers interested in 19th-century travel satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative remarks embedded in a humorous 19th-century travelogue (Mark Twain) about how to judge art, guides, and certain travel practices; useful as informal criteria for art appreciation and traveler behavior. Emphasis is on satirical, observational standards rather than formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of saints in paintings (visual 'trade-marks')
rubrics_metrics.description: When we see a monk going about with a lion and looking tranquilly up to heaven, we know that that is St. Mark. When we see a monk with a book and a pen, looking tranquilly up to heaven, trying to think of a word, we know that that is St. Matthew. When we see a monk sitting on a rock, looking tranquilly up to heaven, with a human skull beside him...we know that that is St. Jerome. When we see a party looking tranquilly up to heaven, unconscious that his body is shot through and through with arrows, we know that that is St. Sebastian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent visual attributes (lion, book & pen, skull, arrows) as 'trade-marks' to identify saints in religious paintings; if a figure lacks a trade-mark, ask who it is (learn by inquiry). The passage offers concrete examples as an informal decoding key and a humorous note about mnemonic brevity (St. Jerome 'always went flying light in the matter of baggage').

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of martyr portraits (low distinctiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To me it seemed that when I had seen one of these martyrs I had seen them all. They all have a marked family resemblance to each other, they dress alike, in coarse monkish robes and sandals, they are all bald headed, they all stand in about the same attitude, and without exception they are gazing heavenward with countenances...full of 'expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims of uniqueness among conventional religious subjects; evaluate whether subject treatment is merely formulaic (same posture, costume, expression). The passage treats repeated motifs as a legitimate reason for diminished interest—museum-fatigue and lack of originality are flagged as negative qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for historical/human-interest pictures over endless martyrs
rubrics_metrics.description: If great Titian had only been gifted with prophecy, and had skipped a martyr, and gone over to England and painted a portrait of Shakspeare...the world down to the latest generations would have forgiven him the lost martyr in the rescued seer. I think posterity could have spared one more martyr for the sake of a great historical picture of Titian's time...such as Columbus returning in chains from the discovery of a world, for instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate paintings that capture notable historical events or vivid human stories more highly than repetitive religious martyrdom scenes. Consider novelty and historical resonance as merits; the passage gives an example (Columbus in chains) as a preferable subject that would have enduring interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of guide-labels: 'of the Renaissance' as a negative cue
rubrics_metrics.description: This very thing has occurred more times than I can mention, in Venice. In every single instance the guide has crushed out my swelling enthusiasm with the remark: 'It is nothing--it is of the Renaissance.' ... We learned, then, that Renaissance was not a man; that renaissance was a term used to signify what was at best but an imperfect rejuvenation of art...an inferior sort of painters sprang up, and these shabby pictures were the work of their hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat guide-comments like 'of the Renaissance' as shorthand indicating a later, less admired school (in Twain's view). Don't accept a label uncritically—learn what a guide's taxonomy implies about quality and provenance; the anecdote cautions that such labels may be used to dismiss works as inferior to the 'old masters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: A good guide: competence and demeanor
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide I have spoken of...was born in South Carolina, of slave parents...He is well educated. He reads, writes, and speaks English, Italian, Spanish, and French, with perfect facility; is a worshipper of art and thoroughly conversant with it; knows the history of Venice by heart and never tires of talking of her illustrious career. He dresses better than any of us, I think, and is daintily polite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess guides by language skills, breadth of historical/art knowledge, genuine enthusiasm for the subject, polished appearance, and courteous manner. Twain uses this composite as an exemplar of an excellent guide—multilingual, erudite, polite, and passionate about art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal enthusiasm is an unreliable indicator of artistic value
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems to me that whenever I glory to think that for once I have discovered an ancient painting that is beautiful and worthy of all praise, the pleasure it gives me is an infallible proof that it is not a beautiful picture and not in any wise worthy of commendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about aesthetic judgment: intense personal excitement can signal personal bias or poor taste; use external criteria (historical importance, technical mastery, consensus) rather than just one's private elation to judge a work's merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum/multiple-exposure fatigue lowers appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: We have seen famous pictures until our eyes are weary with looking at them and refuse to find interest in them any longer. ... I have seen thirteen thousand St. Jeromes, and twenty-two thousand St. Marks, and sixteen thousand St. Matthews, and sixty thousand St. Sebastians, and four millions of assorted monks, undesignated...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that volume and repetition diminish critical sensitivity—limit exposure or curate visits to avoid numbing. The passage treats overexposure as a reason one's appreciation flattens; curatorial selection can preserve interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical craftsmanship and labor/time as evaluative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: They will take particles of stone or glass no larger than a mustard seed...I saw a little table...whose top was made of some sort of precious polished stone, and in the stone was inlaid the figure of a flute...This table-top cost the labor of one man for ten long years, so they said, and it was for sale for thirty-five thousand dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the technical difficulty, minuteness of workmanship, and labor-time investment when judging the value and merit of decorative arts (mosaics, inlays). Use concrete evidence of craft and time spent as part of assessment and pricing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility and practical value as metrics of worth
rubrics_metrics.description: These things win me more than Italy's hundred galleries of priceless art treasures, because I can understand the one and am not competent to appreciate the other. In the turnpikes, the railways, the depots, and the new boulevards...I see the genius of Louis Napoleon...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to works (infrastructure, public works) whose purpose and benefits are comprehensible and demonstrable; when art is inscrutable to the observer, practical achievements may be more appreciable. This is an argument for accessibility as a criterion for value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical evaluation: art's grandeur vs social welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, where is the use of allowing all those riches to lie idle, while half of that community hardly know, from day to day, how they are going to keep body and soul together?...All the churches in an ordinary American city put together could hardly buy the jeweled frippery in one of her hundred cathedrals. And for every beggar in America, Italy can show a hundred--and rags and vermin to match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include moral and social considerations in appraising monumental religious art and church wealth—ask whether resources devoted to ornamentation could be justifiably reallocated to alleviate poverty. The passage uses stark social contrast as a criterion against excessive ecclesiastical lavishness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical traveler conduct: language, identification, and local customs
rubrics_metrics.description: I got lost in Florence...At last, somewhere after one o'clock, I came unexpectedly to one of the city gates. I said: 'Hotel d'Europe!' ... They took me into the guard-house and searched me...I made them a present of [a] small piece of soap...I continued to say Hotel d'Europe, and they continued to shake their heads, until at last a young soldier...said he knew where the hotel was...At that moment it struck me that there was something familiar about the house over the way. It was the hotel!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When traveling, know and be able to communicate the hotel name/local destination in the local language; carry simple tokens/gifts if appropriate; be aware that soldiers/police may not speak your language and that showing clear identification or a locally intelligible name can resolve misunderstandings. The anecdote underscores preparedness and simple communication as practical safety/efficiency criteria.
